extracted.intended_audience: IP policymakers, patent office staff, researchers, and other intellectual property stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, measurement choices, and evaluative indicators used in WIPO's patent statistics (patentability standards, family definitions, examination outcomes, technology and country specialization metrics). Useful for interpreting and comparing patent data across offices and origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices must assess whether the claims presented in an application meet the standards of novelty, non-obviousness and industrial applicability defined in national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processing patents consumes time and resources. Examination procedures differ between offices, which makes cross-country comparison difficult. Do not compare application data for a given year with grant data from the same year. 'Rejection of an application does not mean a final rejection.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent family is a set of interrelated patent applications filed at one or more offices to protect the same invention. Patent applications within a family are interlinked by one or more of the following: priority claim, Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) national phase entry, continuation, continuation-in-part, internal priority, and addition or division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A special subset comprises foreign-oriented patent families — those with at least one filing office different from the office of the applicant’s country of origin. Some foreign-oriented families include only one filing office when applicants file directly at a foreign office (example: a Canadian applicant filing directly with the USPTO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-oriented patent families as quality/value indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-oriented patent families are usually considered to be of higher quality and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing patents in multiple jurisdictions is costly and time-consuming, so applicants tend to be selective about filing outside their domestic jurisdiction. Foreign-oriented families reduce bias toward domestic filings, making them more reliable for cross-country comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications pending (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications pending is defined as all patent applications, at any stage in the process, awaiting a final decision by a patent office, including those applications for which applicants have not filed a request for examination (where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where offices have a large proportion of applications pending a request for examination, the scope to reduce the stock of applications pending is somewhat limited because an office cannot start substantive examination until a request for examination is filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent examination outcome categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examination outcomes are categorised as granted, rejected or withdrawn/abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices differ in shares of each outcome (e.g., grants, rejections, withdrawals vary widely across top offices). The number of patents granted out of total processed should not be interpreted directly as a 'grant rate' without considering selection and process differences across offices. Withdrawn/abandoned and rejected volumes can reflect applicant behaviour and office procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents in force and maintenance/renewal fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A holder must pay a maintenance/renewal fee in order for a patent to remain valid, and may opt to let a patent lapse before the end of its full term. Patent rights generally last for up to 20 years from the date an application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics report patents in force across jurisdictions and by age; e.g., about 35.3% of granted patents remained in force for at least 10 years after filing, and about 17% lasted the full 20-year term. Differences in average age and retention rates across offices are relevant for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model (UM) eligibility and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility model is a special form of patent right granted by a state or jurisdiction to an inventor or the inventor’s assignee for a fixed period of time. The terms and conditions for granting a UM differ slightly from those for normal patents, including a shorter term of protection and less stringent eligibility requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldwide UM filings are heavily concentrated in some origins (e.g., China). Resident applications constitute the vast majority of UM filings. Trends and country composition (resident vs non-resident) matter when using UM counts as an indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Specialization Index (RSI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative specialization index (RSI) is used to focus on specialization patterns of countries across different technology fields; a positive RSI value indicates that a country specializes in a given field (it accounts for a larger share of their total patenting activity compared to the global average).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RSI highlights comparative advantages (examples: China and the US positive in computer technology; Sweden strongly specialized in digital communication; various countries specialize in energy or medical technologies). Use RSI to compare technology focus rather than raw counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-field shares and growth (field distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Published patent applications are categorised by field of technology (e.g., computer technology, electrical machinery, measurement, digital communication, medical technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trend analysis (shares and average annual growth rates) reveals which fields drive aggregate patenting growth (example: computer technology grew 10.3% annually between 2013 and 2023 and reached 13.2% of worldwide published applications). Use field shares together with growth rates and RSI to interpret specialization and technological trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical coverage of patent families (number of offices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution of patent families by number of filing offices indicates the geographical coverage of protection for an invention (single-office vs multi-office families; counts of families covering more than five offices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High shares of multi-office families (e.g., Netherlands, Switzerland) may reflect small domestic markets and many multinationals; very low multi-office shares (e.g., China, Russian Federation) indicate mostly single-office filings. Use coverage as a proxy for internationalization and potential value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident vs non-resident shares (origin composition metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics distinguish resident and non-resident patent applications/grants and patents in force; e.g., shares of patents in force originating from resident or non-resident applicants for each office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These shares affect interpretation of an office's portfolio (some offices have >80–90% non-resident patents in force). Contribution of resident and non-resident filings to growth (year-on-year) is also reported and should be used to understand drivers of activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office procedural metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural metrics include distribution of patent examination outcomes, potentially pending applications, average pendency times for first office action and final decision, number of patent examiners, and average years of experience of patent examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in office capacity, pendency, and examiner experience influence grant volumes and timing; these metrics are essential when comparing offices or explaining changes in grant/output volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) flows
rubrics_metrics.description: PPH requests by office of first filing and offices of later examination, and flows of PPH requests between offices, are tracked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PPH activity measures inter-office cooperation and can indicate how office work-sharing affects examination workload and harmonization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender participation metrics for inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation of women inventors in published PCT applications: share of women among listed inventors and share of applications with at least one woman inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric is reported over time and by field and origin (e.g., women were 18% of inventors in 2024; life-science-related fields show higher shares). Use these metrics to assess diversity trends in innovation.
